articles.title: Did Ukraine Use Pelican Ballistic Missile to Strike Moscow?
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Sept. 20, that Ukrainian forces deployed an array of domestically developed long-range strike systems against strategic targets in Russia overnight, including a ballistic missile designated “Pelican.”
Writing on social media, Zelensky confirmed strikes on critical oil refining and logistics facilities supporting the Russian war effort across the Moscow region and an industrial enterprise in the Voronezh region.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The president specifically listed the weapons deployed by Ukrainian intelligence and military units, identifying the FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sichnevyi, and Pelican.
“In the Moscow region tonight, our long-range responses worked very noticeably,” Zelensky stated. “Key oil industry and logistics facilities supporting the aggressor’s war machine were hit. These represent billions of dollars sustaining the war effort.”
The public inclusion of Pelican among the strike assets ignited widespread technical debate among military observers regarding whether Ukraine has deployed its newly developed FP-7 short-range ballistic missile in combat, and whether it could physically reach the Russian capital.
Range limitations, operational role of the FP-7
Multiple reports have linked the Pelican to Ukrainian arms maker Fire Point’s FP-7, though it’s not entirely clear whether they’re one and the same.
Fico Claims West Seeks NATO-Russia War After ‘Failed’ Ukraine Plan
In September 2025, Ukrainian arms maker Fire Point revealed the development of the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile and the larger FP-9, positioning them as sovereign strike alternatives to foreign systems such as the US-supplied ATACMS – but they were never given a name, save for the model number.
Fire Point previously designated its FP-5 cruise missile as the “Flamingo,” though the name “Pelican” has never been mentioned until Sunday by Zelensky.
Defense analysts caution that the FP-7’s technical specifications make a direct ballistic strike on Moscow highly improbable.
Radio NV military analyst Vasyl Pekhno noted that the FP-7 has an engineered operational range of 200-350 kilometers (124-217 miles), whereas Moscow sits approximately 450-500 kilometers (280-311 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
“There are great doubts that it could fly that far, because its design range is only 350 kilometers,” Pekhno explained. “It cannot reach Moscow directly.”
Pekhno suggested that the ballistic weapon may have played an integral role within a coordinated, multi-axis combined strike.
Under such an operational design, short-range ballistic missiles could engage Russian air defense batteries, such as S-400 radar and launcher sites deployed in border regions like Bryansk or Voronezh, creating localized air defense gaps that allowed slower long-range drones and Flamingo cruise missiles to penetrate deep into metropolitan Moscow.
“If we consider that ballistics were an element of the broader operation, the puzzle comes together,” Pekhno added. “For instance, ballistic missiles could strike S-400 deployment sites while other systems saturated the air defense network, enabling Flamingo missiles to reach their designated targets.”
Development of the FP-7 and long-range FP-9
The FP-7 can be seen as a tactical ballistic missile, while the FP-9 is reserved for deeper strikes.
In February 2026, Fire Point released footage demonstrating the initial test launch of the FP-7. According to technical specifications published by the manufacturer, the ground-launched missile carries a 150-kilogram (331-lb) warhead, has a maximum speed of 1,500 meters per second (3,355 mph), and achieves a reported terminal accuracy deviation of roughly 14 meters (46 feet).
Earlier in September, Fire Point Chief Executive Officer Iryna Terekh announced at the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland that the FP-7 had concluded two phases of operational testing and was preparing for immediate frontline combat deployment within weeks rather than months.
Concurrently, Fire Point has been developing the larger FP-9 ballistic missile, engineered to achieve a reported range of up to 850 kilometers (528 miles).
Fire Point chief designer Denys Shtilerman noted during the summer that flight trials for the 850-kilometer system could involve test trajectories directed toward symbolic Russian targets, given that testing an 850-kilometer missile within Ukrainian airspace is geographically unfeasible.
Both the FP-7 and FP-9 systems were known to be advancing through rapid development and testing cycles over recent months.
While specific technical parameters regarding the Pelican missile mentioned in Zelensky’s statement remain classified, defense assessments indicate that the missile directly impacting metropolitan Moscow is unlikely to be the baseline FP-7 given its 200-300-kilometer range.
At the same time, it remains unconfirmed whether Fire Point has expedited combat trials of the heavier 850-kilometer FP-9 platform, or whether the Pelican designation was applied to an intermediate ballistic variant tailored to strike Russian air defense corridors.
Capital refinery damage and multi-drone saturation
The overnight attack inflicted structural damage on key Russian industrial infrastructure. The General Staff of the Ukrainian military confirmed hits on the Gazprom Neft Moscow Oil Refinery in Moscow’s southeastern Kapotnya district, approximately 15 kilometers (9 miles) from the Kremlin.
According to military authorities, long-range drones operated by the Security Service of Ukraine’s (SBU) “Alpha” Special Operations Center flew over 500 kilometers to breach dense capital air defenses, striking the refinery’s AVT-6 primary crude distillation unit, an integrated refining facility, and an isomerization unit. Geolocation analysis of footage published by metropolitan residents confirmed large fires at the refining site.
The Moscow Oil Refinery processes approximately 11.6 million metric tons of crude oil annually, supplying roughly 40 percent of the fuel requirements for the capital and 70 percent of gasoline and aviation kerosene consumed across the wider Moscow region.
Simultaneously, Fire Point confirmed that its FP-1 attack drones struck and destroyed commercial storage complexes operated by Modern Warehouse Technologies in Sofyino, within the Ramensky district of Moscow region.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that Russian air defenses intercepted more than 1,600 drones across all defensive echelons since Saturday, including 450 downed on approach to the capital, calling the barrage the largest drone assault on Moscow to date.
Moscow Region Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported at least two civilians killed and six injured across the surrounding province.

articles.title: Fico Claims West Seeks NATO-Russia War After ‘Failed’ Ukraine Plan
articles.body:
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico claimed that several Western politicians are actively attempting to provoke a direct military confrontation between NATO and Russia following what he termed a “failed” strategy of supporting Ukraine, Reuters reported.
In a video address published on Saturday, Sept. 19, the Slovak leader warned that Europe is closer to a full-scale continental war than at any point in modern history, asserting that Western nations are exacerbating regional tensions by sustaining military backing for Kyiv without achieving tangible results.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are facing a mortal danger,” Fico stated, arguing that Western partners have continued “adding fuel to the fire” through prolonged military assistance.
“The failure of the strategy to destroy Russia through the war in Ukraine has led some Western politicians to believe that if this goal cannot be achieved with the help of the Ukrainian army and its full support, then every effort must be made to provoke a conflict between NATO and Russia,” Fico said.
The Slovak prime minister insisted that the ongoing armed conflict in Ukraine is neither Slovakia’s war nor NATO’s war, arguing that Bratislava must avoid being drawn into direct confrontation with Moscow.
Questioning Article 5
Fico’s latest assertions follow previous public interventions in which he questioned whether Slovakia should uphold its obligations under NATO’s collective defense architecture.
Russia Fired 2,000 Drones and 19 Missiles This Week, Zelensky Says
Speaking earlier to students and medical staff in the eastern Slovak city of Prešov, Fico criticized what he described as increasingly belligerent rhetoric among European heads of state, questioning the strategic rationale for collective defense preparations and asking whom European nations intend to fight.
“Can you imagine, ladies and gentlemen, that Article 5 of the NATO treaty would be invoked?” Fico told the gathering in Prešov. “Can anyone imagine that we would be told: Prepare 5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers, and they will go somewhere to fight? And we would not even know with whom, why, or for what?”
Fico pledged that his administration would do “everything” to insulate the country from any military escalation, declaring that he would not permit Slovak armed forces to be deployed under allied collective defense mechanisms.
Under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty – to which Slovakia acceded in 2004 – an armed attack against one member state is treated as an attack against all allies.
However, NATO statutory provisions do not mandate automatic troop deployments or predetermined force quotas; each individual member state retains sovereign discretion to determine the specific assistance it deems necessary, which may range from logistics and intelligence sharing to direct military force.
Slovak foreign policy recalibration
Fico’s criticism of Western defense posture marks the continuation of a calibrated shift in Bratislava’s foreign policy following his return to office as head of a left-nationalist coalition government in late 2023.
Since assuming leadership, Fico has halted state-funded military aid packages to Ukraine, opposed European sanctions against Moscow’s energy sector, and consistently advocated for immediate diplomatic negotiations that would leave occupied Ukrainian territories under Russian control.
In May, Fico became one of the few European heads of government to attend official Victory Day commemorations in Moscow alongside EVladimir Putin.
Despite the cessation of state-directed military donations from Slovak armed forces stockpiles, Fico’s cabinet has permitted Slovak defense contractors to continue commercial weapons manufacturing and export contracts with Ukraine, including serial production lines for 155mm Zuzana 2 self-propelled howitzers and heavy artillery ammunition.

articles.title: Europe gave Russia years to perfect its aerial killing. Ukraine is paying the price. Europe may be next.
articles.body:
For years, Ukraine’s air defenses blunted Russia’s attempts to terrorize its cities from the sky. Now, after four years of adaptation, Moscow is fielding faster drones, massing ballistic missiles, and finding new ways to overwhelm a Ukrainian air-defense network running short of the interceptors needed to stop them.
Russia’s aerial campaign is becoming harder to contain just as its attacks are killing more Ukrainian civilians. July recorded at least 437 civilian deaths, the highest monthly toll since the early months of the full-scale invasion, with UN monitors pointing to Russian missile and drone attacks as a key factor.
That shift is visible most clearly in Russia’s rapidly expanding use of jet-powered Geran drones. These drones can exceed 400 km/h, making them significantly harder to intercept than the slower, propeller-driven Shaheds Ukraine has spent years learning to counter. Russia reportedly launched as many as 2,850 jet-powered drones in August alone.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Russia’s escalation with the new drones is becoming “increasingly terrorist” and called for urgent efforts to develop defenses against them.
While Ukraine’s Western partners have taken steps to strengthen its air defenses, Russia has spent the same period adapting and expanding its ability to attack from the air. The gap is becoming increasingly visible in the skies over Ukrainian cities.
Ukrainian civilians are already paying the price
Russia has increasingly turned its ability to strike deep inside Ukraine into a weapon against civilian life itself: hitting residential areas, fuel stations, railways, energy infrastructure and other sites across cities far from the front.
Since late August, Kyiv has faced near-continuous Russian drone attacks, with Russia increasingly sending waves of drones against the capital throughout the day and night. The shift has made air-raid alerts, explosions and disruptions to daily life a near-constant reality.
For Ukrainians, Russia’s evolving aerial campaign is measured in destroyed homes, injuries, deaths, and lives permanently changed.
In Kyiv, it has also changed everyday life: explosions interrupt sleep and work, people run for shelter as strikes unfold overhead, and the threat of another attack is never far away.
And the pressure is no longer confined to Kyiv. Kharkiv, Odesa, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia are all facing increasingly sophisticated combinations of drones and missiles.
The danger is not simply that Russia is launching more weapons. It is that Moscow has spent years learning which weapons can penetrate Ukraine’s defenses, how to combine them, and how to force Ukraine to spend its most valuable interceptors.
Zelenskyy’s warning captures the urgency: “You cannot simply wait for Russia to perfect its repertoire of killings.”
Russia is adapting faster than Ukraine can rebuild its shield
The jet-powered Geran is only one part of the problem.
Russia has also dramatically increased its use of ballistic missiles. Reuters reported that 228 ballistic and hypersonic missiles were launched in July and the first eight days of August, with more than half being inaccurate RM48U training missiles repurposed for combat.
Ukraine has virtually exhausted its US-made Patriot interceptors, the only systems in its arsenal capable of reliably intercepting Russia’s ballistic missiles, while Moscow continues launching them at a high tempo.
The result is a more complex aerial threat: fast drones that are difficult to intercept, ballistic missiles that are extremely difficult to stop, and large waves of cheaper weapons that can force Ukraine to expend scarce defensive ammunition.
Trending Now
Ukraine is developing new ways to counter them, including interceptor drones specifically designed to hunt down the jet-powered Gerans. But Ukraine is developing these systems as Russia is already deploying its new weapons at scale.
Western countries have continued providing air-defense assistance. Canada, for example, announced a C$350 million package for interceptors earlier this month. But Ukrainian officials continue to say that deliveries remain far below what is needed to protect the country from Russia’s expanding aerial campaign.
Russia has spent years expanding the weapons it can use against Ukraine, while Ukraine and its partners are still racing to develop and supply the systems needed to stop them.
The threat Europe helped Russia develop
Some of Ukraine’s Western partners are now confronting a threat Russia has spent years developing over Ukraine: an increasingly sophisticated aerial arsenal that could eventually be turned against them.
European officials and defense analysts are increasingly warning that NATO countries themselves lack enough air and missile defenses to deal with a large Russian attack.
Latvia’s President Edgars Rinkēvičs recently said Europe is not sufficiently prepared for the kind of drone and aerial warfare Russia has developed in Ukraine, including because of delays in supplying Ukraine with critical air-defense systems.
Those concerns are no longer hypothetical. On 14 September, an Italian NATO fighter jet shot down a Russian-made Geran-2 drone over Lithuania after it entered the country from Belarus. Poland and Romania have also faced Russian drone incursions since 2025.
This creates a problem that is partly of Europe’s own making. Russia has had more than four years to refine its drones, missiles, production lines and tactics while Ukraine’s partners have often been too slow to provide enough weapons to counter those systems as they were developed and deployed at scale.
In that same period, many European countries continued trading with Russia, particularly in fossil fuels, allowing Moscow to keep generating revenue from European markets even as those same governments were providing military aid to Ukraine.
The result is a Russian aerial arsenal that is more capable than the one Ukraine faced in 2022 – while some of the countries now worried about a future Russian threat lack the air defenses needed to protect themselves.
Western governments helped Ukraine fight Russia’s air war, but not at a scale or speed sufficient to prevent Russia from adapting.
Ukrainian civilians are paying the price for the time Russia was given to expand and refine its aerial warfare. Now, Europe is having to prepare for the possibility that those capabilities could one day be used against it.

articles.title: Weak Ukraine Air Defense Threatens Poland, Defense Chief Warns
articles.body:
Failing to supply Ukraine with sufficient air defense systems and interceptor ammunition directly increases the military threat to Poland, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned.
Speaking before lawmakers, Kosiniak-Kamysz stated that Polish fighter jets were scrambled again overnight to secure national airspace amid Russian missile and drone barrages targeting western Ukraine. The defense minister emphasized that recurring incidents along NATO’s eastern frontier can no longer be interpreted as accidental deviations.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“These are no longer isolated incidents; this is planned aggression against NATO member states. It is not an accident, it is the strategy of the Russian Federation,” Kosiniak-Kamysz told parliament, as reported by broadcaster TVN24.
Kosiniak-Kamysz criticized opposition parliamentarians over statements questioning defense aid to Kyiv, arguing that rhetoric seeking to curb military assistance aligns with Moscow’s strategic objectives rather than Poland’s national security interests.
“Missiles fall and drones fall one kilometer from the Polish border,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said. “If Ukraine does not have air defense assets, if it does not have ammunition to shoot down these drones, most of these drones will fly through Ukraine and reach Poland. Is that what you want?”
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 19, 2026
Border drone threats
The defense minister’s remarks followed an address by Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of the right-wing Confederation (Konfederacja) party. Mentzen had criticized the condition of Poland’s armed forces, pointing to shortages in domestic artillery ammunition reserves, deficiencies in reserve personnel training, and inadequate civil defense and bomb shelter infrastructure.
Responding to the criticism, Kosiniak-Kamysz insisted that sustaining Ukraine’s frontline interception capability remains the most effective operational barrier preventing Russian aerial munitions from penetrating deeper into allied territory.
The debate in Warsaw coincides with a series of cross-border security alerts along Poland’s eastern frontier.
On Sept. 13, Russian munitions struck within two kilometers of the Polish border in the Volyn region, damaging a commercial filling station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk checkpoint and hitting the locomotive of a passenger train operating on the Kyiv-Warsaw rail corridor.
Polish air defenses and allied aircraft stationed along NATO’s eastern flank have repeatedly entered elevated readiness postures to monitor incoming Russian strike waves, with military planners cautioning that the deployment of high-speed jet-powered drones increases the margin of error near international boundaries.
Regional missile defense integration
The parliamentary debate follows Poland’s formal accession to a European defense coalition dedicated to countering ballistic missile threats alongside Ukraine and nine other European nations.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Poland’s participation during a joint press conference in Ukraine on Friday, Sept. 18.
Tusk characterized Poland’s initial omission from the initiative’s July launch in Paris as an administrative misunderstanding that has been resolved, noting that Polish defense enterprises are reviewing options to contribute industrially to joint interceptor programs.
The coalition encompasses Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, the UK and Ukraine, aiming to establish collaborative production lines and integrate regional radar architectures.
During their bilateral talks, Tusk and Zelensky also discussed the formation of the “Carpathian Eight,” a proposed regional security and economic format designed to reinforce infrastructure resilience and institutional alignment between Central European states and the EU.

articles.title: Russia is Attacking Europe: Let’s Stop Calling it ‘Hybrid’
articles.body:
Let’s stop calling Russian attacks against Europe hybrid attacks. The phrase has become a political sedative. It allows governments to acknowledge Russian aggression while placing it in a category that sits safely below war, Article 5 and any meaningful retaliation.
Let’s call them what they are: acoordinated Russian campaign of covert, warlike attacks, designed to discover how much violence Europe will absorb without imposing a price.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The problem is that each attack is treated as a separate incident against a separate country. The evidence is investigated nationally, the condemnation is issued nationally and any response is left to the country attacked. The campaign against Europe is broken into isolated cases, making a collective response politically much harder.
And it is a collective response that is the best way to respond to these attacks and force Russia into some kind of restraint. Europe should treat every confidently attributed Russian operation as part of an attack on European security, then select a collective and proportionate response from an agreed ladder of measures.
Europe is hardly out of options. It can tighten sanctions, freeze more assets, expel Russian operatives, launch cyber operations and put pressure on the countries helping Moscow, especially China. Further up the ladder come intercepting Russian drones and missiles, protecting western Ukraine from the air and, in the gravest circumstances, direct NATO action.
Largest Drone Strike on Moscow Hits Oil Refinery and Logistics Hub
Most attacks would be answered far below the top rung. A no-fly zone or direct military action would remain emergency options. Keeping them on the table does not mean reaching for them now.
Europe sees incidents but for Russia it’s a campaign
The term “hybrid” once described a useful fact. Russia mixes sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, political interference and deniable kinetic attacks. Sure, the mix is hybrid but the political effect of the label has changed.
It makes acts of violence sound ambiguous, manageable and somehow less real. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys put it plainly: “Russia’s attacks against us are no longer hybrid. They are very kinetic.”
Radosław Sikorski, the Polish foreign minister, spoke in a similar vein, saying on Thursday that “Russia’s hybrid war against Europe has already taken on a ‘kinetic’ dimension” and that these are “on the border between hybrid warfare and outright aggression.”
It’s almost war
The evidence is accumulating. Germany has attributed the explosive-drone attack at Leipzig-Halle airport to Russia. European authorities have investigated suspected Russian sabotage against defense companies and infrastructure in Poland, Estonia and Slovakia. Russia has also been linked to cyberattacks, interference with railways and energy systems, threats to undersea infrastructure and repeated violations of NATO airspace.
The Institute for the Study of War, a US based think-tank, says: “The Kremlin is conducting these actions against Europe as part of a series of mutually supporting kinetic and cognitive campaigns.”
Each attack is also as if the Kremlin is checking the cost it has to pay for each provocation. The results have been encouraging for Russia. Poland responded to the Russian-directed railway bombing by closing Moscow’s last consulate in Gdańsk. Germany answered the Leipzig attack by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin. Russia retaliated by closing Germany’s consulate in St Petersburg and its Goethe-Institut centers.
These actions imposed some cost. They were still national and easy for Moscow to absorb. Neither attack automatically brought an EU-wide sanctions package, coordinated expulsions or additional weapons for Ukraine. The extra European cost was effectively zero.
The real target is collective defense
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that Russia could strike NATO territory and then present the incident as “accidental”. The official story, he said, would be that there was no reason to consider a NATO response.
That’s the point. Russia wants Article 5 to appear, in Tusk’s words, “more theoretical than practical”. The immediate target may be a train, factory, airport or undersea cable but the strategic target is the credibility of collective defense. The Kremlin also wants to break European unity and wear down support for Ukraine.
NATO already accepts that a hybrid operation could, in some circumstances, trigger Article 5. The obstacle is political. Allies examine each incident separately, so almost every operation appears too small to justify a collective response.
Europe must reverse that calculation. An attack intended to divide European countries should bring them closer together. An operation designed to weaken Ukraine support should automatically produce more weapons, funding or air defense for Ukraine. Every Russian attempt to frighten one country should trigger a visible response from all.
That would send Moscow a message it could understand. These attacks are failing. They are strengthening European unity, increasing the cost to Russia and delivering more support to the country the Kremlin is trying to destroy.
Russia may be ready before Europe
The danger extends beyond sabotage. “According to all our sources, late autumn and winter will be the most critical moment so far in the Russian-Ukrainian war,” Donald Tusk told parliament. He warned that Russia could extend the pressure to NATO’s eastern flank through supposedly “accidental” drone or missile strikes designed to paralyze the alliance’s response.
Europe is rearming, but many of its new forces, factories and air-defense systems will not be ready until 2029. Meanwhile, Washington wants Europe to take greater responsibility for conventional defense, and the Pentagon is considering a substantial reduction in US forces on the continent, even by as much as 50%, according to the latest reports from NBC.
Russia also retains an effective army despite its slow progress in Ukraine. It has battle-hardened troops, a wartime arms industry and growing experience with drones, missiles and infiltration tactics.
Russia would not need the strength to conquer Europe. A limited incursion, drone strike or missile attack could be enough to test whether NATO could agree on an Article 5 response.
NATO provides the shield. The EU sets the price
NATO remains Europe’s main instrument for military deterrence and defense. The EU controls many of the economic tools most useful after sabotage or a cyberattack, including sanctions, asset freezes, export controls and defense financing.
The problem is that these powers are divided. NATO cannot impose sanctions, the EU cannot command NATO forces, and security powers such as Britain and Norway sit outside the EU.
Ursula von der Leyen has proposed three ways to connect them. A counter-hybrid playbook would list the available responses. An Emergency Security Protocol could be triggered by one EU member and force all 27 to consult. A European Security Council would bring key non-EU partners, including Britain, Norway, Ukraine and Canada, into the political discussion.
The playbook would provide the options, the protocol would trigger the process and the Security Council would build the coalition. The council could still become another talking shop. Its value would depend on governments agreeing the response ladder in advance and arriving ready to act.

articles.title: US warns of Mideast escalation after Houthis strike Saudi capital
articles.body:
The U.S. has warned that hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthis could “escalate rapidly” after a Saturday missile targeted Riyadh for the first time since Yemen’s civil war resumed.
President Donald Trump cut short a weekend at Camp David, a secluded presidential complex in rural Maryland, to return unexpectedly to the White House on Saturday.
The White House gave no explanation for the early return, which came as the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis crossed a new threshold. The Houthis control a large part of Yemen and are fighting government forces backed by a coalition led by Riyadh.
Loud explosions rang out twice Saturday in the Saudi capital, where a fuel tank bearing the logo of oil giant Aramco was on fire near the airport, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).
"This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly," the U.S. State Department warned, adding American citizens outside the Middle East should "seriously reconsider travel to and through the region."
The Houthis' lightning offensive seizing large areas of Yemeni territory in recent weeks has left hundreds killed and, according to the U.N., displaced over 110,000 people.
These clashes and the subsequent hostilities with the kingdom have already disrupted Saudi Arabia's exports – the world's leading supplier of crude oil – as well as maritime traffic.
The Riyadh-led coalition confirmed Saturday evening in a post on X that a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward the capital was "successfully intercepted and destroyed."
The coalition added that the pro-Iranian fighters had tried to target "civilians and civilian infrastructure" in several cities in the west of the kingdom, including the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, an important export hub for Saudi oil.
It said these attacks were "thwarted by the kingdom's air defenses."
Saudi Arabia has responded with scores of airstrikes on Houthi-held areas but failed to stop the advance.
The Houthis said they had responded to recent Saudi attacks by carrying out "two successful military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement on Telegram.
"The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu."
Saudi authorities had earlier issued an overnight air raid alert.
Hours after the early morning alert, residents told AFP anonymously that they heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.
This is the first time since Yemen's civil war resumed that strikes have threatened the Saudi capital, piling further pressure on a global economy already rocked by seven months of war between the U.S. and Iran.
Riyadh residents received a message just before 3 a.m. urging them to stay indoors and warning, "The area is under a hostile aerial threat."
AFP reported two explosions, before the Saudi civil defense agency lifted the alert 30 minutes later.
"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," a Riyadh resident said. Another resident described the attack as "terrifying."
The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca Wednesday, denouncing it as a "cowardly terrorist attack" on Islam's holy city, which welcomes millions of pilgrims each year. The Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a "worn-out lie."
The group has reported scores of retaliatory strikes carried out daily by Riyadh since their offensive this month to take over the country's entire Red Sea coast, giving them control over the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The United States, according to U.S. news platform Axios, last week refused a Saudi request to strike the Houthis.
Washington approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to the kingdom Thursday to help Riyadh "deter current and future threats," the U.S. State Department said.
Yemen's civil war broke out in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the capital Sana and other regions, triggering a military intervention led by Saudi Arabia in March 2015.
The fragile truce reached in 2022 between the warring parties collapsed in July, when the Houthis defied Riyadh's control of Yemeni airspace by allowing an Iranian aircraft to land in Yemen.
The apparent attack came as the Houthis improve their defenses in newly conquered territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline, with members of the group telling AFP they have been installing radar and digging tunnels.

articles.title: ‘Conflict has potential to escalate rapidly’: US issues Mideast warnings as Trump leaves Camp David early
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House earlier than expected from Camp David on Saturday as fighting in Yemen escalated following a Houthi ballistic missile attack targeting the Saudi capital, Riyadh.
The White House gave no explanation for Trump’s early return from the presidential retreat in Maryland, a day before he had originally been scheduled to leave. His return came as the United States issued another series of warnings about tensions in the Middle East, this time specifically citing the Houthis alongside Iran.
“Due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation,” the U.S. warning said, urging Americans in the region to remain vigilant and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.
The warning said the Iran-backed Houthis were engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks affecting civilian airports, and cautioned that the conflict could escalate rapidly.
The State Department urged Americans to reconsider travel to or through the Middle East. It also reiterated that U.S. diplomatic facilities, including those outside the region, have previously been targeted and warned that Iran and Iran-aligned groups could target other U.S. interests, businesses, institutions and citizens overseas.
Warnings were issued by U.S. embassies across the region, including in Israel, Oman, Lebanon, Iraq, Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Saudi Arabia said the Houthi attack on Riyadh involved a ballistic missile that was intercepted. Residents reported hearing explosions, and flames and thick smoke were seen near the airport. Saudi authorities reported no casualties or damage from the missile itself.
The Saudi-led coalition also said the Houthis attempted to strike civilian infrastructure in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, as well as Taif, Baysh and Farasan, but that those attacks were thwarted. Yanbu is a crucial outlet for Saudi oil exports.
The Houthis offered a different account, saying they had attacked “sensitive sites” in Riyadh and facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in Yanbu. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the strikes caused major fires. The claims were not independently verified.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, meanwhile, said Tehran would not return to the previous terms for negotiations with Washington or allow normal passage through the Strait of Hormuz until Iran’s demands were met and the United States honored its commitments.
Iran lays out its conditions
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Qatar’s Al Jazeera on Saturday that Tehran was prepared for what he called a “decisive war” while saying Iran had presented the Trump administration with seven conditions for reopening negotiations.
Rezaei also said Iran’s current nuclear doctrine remained unchanged and that Tehran continued to abide by a religious decree prohibiting nuclear weapons, though he suggested future developments could affect its position.
“Trump’s threats will not achieve any results,” Rezaei told Al Jazeera. “We are prepared for a decisive war.”
Rezaei said Iran was in contact with mediators Qatar and Pakistan and that Doha had relayed Tehran’s conditions to Washington. He said Iran was awaiting Trump’s response.
The publicly disclosed conditions include ending the war on all fronts, releasing frozen Iranian funds and lifting the U.S. naval blockade restricting Iranian oil exports. Tehran has not publicly detailed all seven demands.
The demands resemble conditions Iran previously raised in connection with restrictions on passage through the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway through which a significant share of the world’s oil trade normally passes.
The United States has been conducting operations aimed at protecting shipping and maintaining the flow of oil through the region as the conflict has disrupted energy markets and kept crude prices elevated.
The escalation has increasingly drawn the Houthis into the wider regional confrontation. The group has launched missile and one-way attack drone strikes against Saudi oil and energy infrastructure, while Saudi Arabia has carried out waves of airstrikes against Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen as it supports forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
Saree confirmed that the Houthis launched their first attack on Riyadh since the latest escalation overnight Friday into Saturday. He said the group struck “sensitive sites” in the Saudi capital and an Aramco facility in Yanbu.
Yanbu has become increasingly important to Saudi Arabia as an alternative outlet for oil exports amid severe disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi energy infrastructure has also faced attacks elsewhere during the regional conflict, adding to concerns over the reliability of alternative export routes.
The Houthis said their attacks were retaliation for continuing Saudi airstrikes in Yemen. Saree claimed Saudi Arabia had carried out 732 airstrikes since the latest escalation, a figure that could not be independently verified.
The Houthi spokesman also rejected Saudi allegations that the group had launched a drone toward Mecca, Islam’s holiest city, calling the accusation false. Saudi Arabia had accused the Houthis of targeting the city earlier in the week, an allegation the group denied.
Saree said the Houthis would continue what he described as a policy of “blockade for blockade” and “escalation for escalation” until Saudi attacks ended and restrictions imposed on Houthi-controlled Yemen were lifted.
The Houthis have long accused Saudi Arabia of imposing an air and sea blockade on areas under their control. Even before the latest escalation, the group had announced what it called a naval blockade targeting Saudi shipping.
It remains unclear how the renewed Saudi-Houthi fighting will affect the broader confrontation involving Iran and the United States. The Houthis, who are aligned with Tehran but maintain their own leadership and decision-making structure, have made rapid territorial gains in Yemen in recent weeks and expanded their position along the Red Sea coast.
The escalation has heightened concerns over both Saudi oil exports and shipping through the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandab, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints.
Former U.S. diplomat Joey Hood told CNN that Houthi advances in the Red Sea could strengthen Iran’s position in its broader confrontation with Washington and complicate attempts to negotiate with Tehran.
“Iran is now in an existential struggle and is mobilizing all its proxies to fight,” Hood said, according to CNN. He added that while the Houthis are not remotely controlled by Tehran, they rely on Iranian support, meaning their stated reasons for launching the current offensive may not fully explain the timing of the escalation.

articles.title: Ukraine’s long-range strikes reach Moscow’s fuel supply as Russia votes in State Duma elections
articles.body:
Ukraine launched a massive long-range drone attack on Moscow and Moscow Oblast overnight on 20 September, striking a major Russian oil refinery and a logistics facility, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Ukraine is increasingly targeting Russian oil refineries, logistics hubs, and other strategic infrastructure that helps generate the fuel, revenue, and supplies Russia needs to sustain its war against Ukraine. Striking them allows Kyiv to put pressure on Russia’s war economy and military logistics far beyond the front line.
The Moscow Oil Refinery was among the facilities hit. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin confirmed that an object at the refinery was damaged, while OSINT analysis by ASTRA of eyewitness footage also identified the refinery as one of the attack’s targets.
Zelenskyy said the strikes were carried out using a range of Ukrainian long-range weapons and targeted infrastructure that generates revenue for Russia’s war effort.
The attack took place on the second day of Russia’s three-day State Duma elections, with voting taking place across the country from 19 to 21 September.
Moscow refinery targeted
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces struck “one of the key enterprises of the Russian oil industry” in the Moscow region, along with a logistics facility.
The Moscow Oil Refinery is operated by Gazprom Neft and is located in Moscow’s Kapotnya district. According to information cited by ASTRA, it can process 11 million tons of oil annually and supplies about 40% of Moscow’s fuel market and 70% of the Moscow region’s gasoline and aviation fuel needs.
Sobyanin said an object on the refinery’s territory was damaged and that there were no casualties there.
Ukraine’s long-range campaign
Zelenskyy said Ukraine used FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sich, and Pelican systems in the operation.
He thanked the Security Service of Ukraine, Unmanned Systems Forces, Special Operations Forces, military intelligence, and Foreign Intelligence Service for their involvement.
“The billions of dollars” generated by such facilities help sustain Russia’s military machine, Zelenskyy said, framing the strikes as part of Ukraine’s effort to reduce Russia’s ability to finance and wage its war.
He also said Moscow should end its war rather than build layered air defenses using systems taken from other Russian regions.
Russian authorities report casualties
Russian officials claimed the overnight attack caused two deaths and six injuries across Moscow Oblast.
Governor Andrei Vorobyov claimed Russian air defenses and electronic warfare systems intercepted or suppressed 249 drones across 17 municipal districts between 3 and 5 a.m.
Vorobyov also claimed that a drone strike in Sofyino damaged six apartments in a three-story building, killing a 44-year-old woman and injuring five people. Another person was reportedly killed in a private house in the Orekhovo-Zuyevsky district.
In Ramenskoye, Russian authorities reported a fire at a 21-story apartment building and said about 400 people were evacuated.
Sobyanin separately claimed that the attack was intended to disrupt Russia’s State Duma elections, which were taking place on 20 September. Ukrainian authorities did not say that this was the purpose of the strikes.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Buk-M3, Nebo-U Radar, and Drone Site
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a Russian Buk-M3 surface-to-air missile system, a Nebo-U long-range surveillance radar, an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) manufacturing facility, and frontline command installations across occupied territories on Sept. 19-20.
According to the official military dispatch by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), Ukrainian precision fire engaged high-value Russian air defense and reconnaissance assets deployed across three eastern and southern provinces.

In the Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Buk-M3 medium-range surface-to-air missile complex deployed near the settlement of Ukrainka. The Buk-M3 system is among Russia’s modernized mobile air defense assets designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and combat aircraft.
In the Donetsk region, a precision strike targeted and damaged a Russian Nebo-U early-warning radar station operating in the vicinity of Balka. The Nebo-U system operates in the Very High Frequency (VHF) band and is engineered to detect, identify, and track aerodynamic and ballistic targets, including low-radar-cross-section aircraft and missiles, at ranges of several hundred kilometers.
Concurrently in the Luhansk region, Ukrainian units engaged an industrial facility utilized by Russian forces for manufacturing attack drones near the occupied city of Severodonetsk.

Ukrainian forces also struck tactical command nodes in the Donetsk region, hitting a Russian command and observation post near Zoryane and destroying a UAV control station located in the vicinity of Staromykhailivka.
Sustained campaign against Russian drone nodes and logistics
The overnight strikes follow consecutive Ukrainian precision engagements on Sept. 18-19 aimed at dismantling Russian tactical drone infrastructure, command nodes, and supply hubs in active operational zones.
In those operations, Ukrainian forces targeted multiple UAV control posts in the Zaporizhzhia region, striking command nodes near Volodymyrivka, Verbove, Dobropillya, and Rivnopillya, alongside two separate drone control installations near Novoprokopivka.
Ukrainian artillery and missile units additionally hit the Russian military’s “Vostochny” training range near the occupied settlement of Novopetrivka in the Zaporizhzhia region.
In the Donetsk region, earlier strikes hit Russian UAV command posts near Luhanske and Pokrovsk, while long-range fire struck a material and technical supply warehouse in Rybynske and an ammunition storage depot near Amvrosiivka.
The General Staff also confirmed battle damage assessments from cross-border strikes conducted earlier in the week, verifying that a Ukrainian strike on Sept. 17 damaged a Russian 80P6 surveillance radar station deployed near Mityuli in Russia’s Smolensk region.

articles.title: North Korea launches missiles as it dials up pressure against U.S.
articles.body:
North Korea launches missiles as it dials up pressure against U.S.
North Korea launched two short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea on Sunday, South Korea's military said.
The launches came just days after Pyongyang reasserted its status as a nuclear-armed state and rejected a United Nations resolution demanding it halt its nuclear activities. They were also the latest in a series of weapons demonstrations even after President Trump scaled back a joint military exercise with South Korea last month in an apparent effort to revive diplomacy with the North's leader, Kim Jong Un.
The two missile launches — about three hours apart — were conducted from North Korea's eastern coastal Wonsan area. The first missile flew about 280 miles while the second one flew more than 370 miles, both toward the North's eastern waters, South Korea's military said.
"South Korean and U.S. authorities are conducting a detailed analysis to determine its exact specifications," South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said of the second missile.
The missiles eventually ended up in the sea.
U.S. Pacific Command said in a statement that it was aware of North Korea's missile launches and is "consulting closely with our allies and partners."
"Based on current assessments, these events do not pose an immediate threat to U.S. personnel or territory, or to our allies," it said in a post on X. "The United States remains committed to the defense of the U.S. homeland and our allies in the region."
South Korea's presidential office urged North Korea to immediately halt ballistic missile launches that are banned by U.N. Security Council resolutions. The South's military said it maintains readiness to repel any provocations by the North under a solid alliance with the U.S.
Japan's Defense Ministry said it detected a suspected North Korean missile earlier Sunday but that the weapon did not land in its territorial waters.
Kim's sister and senior official, Kim Yo Jong, earlier shrugged off Mr. Trump's overture, saying that shortening the drill wouldn't change its "provocative, aggressive nature." North Korea's military later launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea, apparently following through with a previous threat to respond to the U.S.-South Korean drill.
On Friday, Kim's sister slammed another recent U.S.-led multilateral maritime exercise in the region as a "frantic military move" by the Americans meant to prolong their hegemony in the Asia-Pacific area. The "Pacific Vanguard" exercise brought together the U.S., South Korea, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and Canada.
She claimed that "regular U.S.-led war rehearsals" are the main source of worsening tensions in the Korean Peninsula and the region.
"Our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence," she said.
Earlier this month, North Korea conducted what it called a joint live-fire drill involving missiles, artillery and drones, a day after the United States, South Korea and Japan wrapped their five-day trilateral military drill that North Korea described as a provocation. North Korea said its drill included firing different types of weapons simultaneously, likely aiming at developing the ability to overwhelm South Korean and U.S. air defenses.

articles.title: North Korea fires two ballistic missiles into the sea in latest weapons display
articles.body:
North Korea fires two ballistic missiles into the sea in latest weapons display
North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles into the sea off its eastern coast on Sunday, South Korea’s military said. This came days after Pyongyang reaffirmed its status as a nuclear-armed state and rejected a UN resolution calling for an end to its nuclear activities.
North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles into the sea off its eastern coast on Sunday, South Korea's military said, with the second flying more than 600 kilometres (370 miles).
The launches came days after Pyongyang reasserted its status as a nuclear-armed state and rejected a United Nations resolution demanding it halt its nuclear activities.

articles.title: North Korea launches 'suspected ballistic missile' into East Sea
articles.body:
In August, Trump told reporters that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un had "57 very powerful nuclear weapons" as he once again touted the pair's relationship.
North Korea on Sunday carried out a launch of a "suspected ballistic missile," the Japanese Prime Minister's office said, while South Korea's military reported that Pyongyang had fired an "unidentified projectile" into the East Sea.
In an update later in the day, Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said North Korea had launched "at least one ballistic missile from near its eastern coast towards the northeast" at around 3 pm local time.
"We estimate that the ballistic missile reached a maximum altitude of approximately 60 km, flew a distance of approximately 440 km, and fell outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ)," he said.
It comes after North Korea this week rejected a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against its nuclear programme.
A spokesperson for the country's Foreign Ministry said the International Atomic Energy Agency's resolution had "no effect on the DPRK's position as a nuclear weapons state."
In August, Trump told reporters that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un had "57 very powerful nuclear weapons" as he once again touted the pair's relationship.
"You know what, the fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing," Trump said, adding that Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal should "never" have been allowed to happen.
Trump announced at the time that he also intended to meet with Kim later this year, although he gave no further details on the plan - which would be their first meeting since Trump's first term in the White House.
On Friday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said he was "urging" Trump to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang, adding that Seoul was working to facilitate talks between the North and the US.
"I cannot say for certain how likely it is, but it is also clear that we must make every possible effort to turn that possibility into reality," he said of the potential for a meeting between US and North Korean officials.
However, hopes for an imminent meeting may have been doused slightly after Kim's powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, criticised recent military drills in the Western Pacific, which she labelled a "US-led war rehearsal."
The US, South Korea and Japan wrapped up Exercise Freedom Edge 26, which US Pacific Command said advanced "trilateral readiness across the Indo-Pacific," on 11 September.
"Our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence," Kim Yo Jong added in a statement shared by North Korea's KCNA state news agency on Friday.

articles.title: European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato
articles.body:
European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”.
The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented”, and on Friday summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting in Paris, where they discussed – among other topics – intelligence of a growing threat from Russia.
The escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine. Kyiv hit Moscow and other Russian regions with hundreds of drones and missiles in the early hours of Sunday, in one of its biggest air attacks of the war.
In separate interviews with the Guardian over the past week, in different locations, three European intelligence leaders discussed their views of the potential threat from Moscow.
Michal Koudelka, the head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, said that as well as increased drone activity, a small-scale invasion of Nato territory that bordered Russia could be part of the Kremlin’s plans. “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said, in a rare interview at the agency’s headquarters in Prague. He said this scenario could play out in a matter of “months, not years” but added that “a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn’t happen”.
Officials in the three Baltic countries, which border Russian territory, have been more cautious about the prospect of an invasion or other serious escalation, citing Moscow’s stretched resources in Ukraine and warning that playing up the prospect of an attack might play into the Kremlin’s hands.
“We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” said Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service, in an interview at the agency’s headquarters in Riga. He conceded there were signs that Moscow was making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans were simply part of a destabilisation strategy.
“It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said.
Baltic politicians, who for many years criticised western Europe for being soft on Russia, now find themselves in the strange position of telling some western leaders to calm down in their public messaging, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could prove damaging to their societies and economies.
On Saturday, the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, decried “panic on social media” in recent days about a possible attack. “If there is reason to fear an attack, rest assured: we will make that clear. Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine,” he wrote on X.
Mežviets said that, overall, it was good that western Europe had woken up to the threat from Russia. “Before 2022, we constantly warned our western European partners about the threat from Russia, but most of the time our voices were not listened to. In 2022, the approach of our partners changed. They said it turns out the Balts and the Poles had been right,” he said.
Neither Mežviets nor Koudelka would discuss what specific intelligence might have been obtained about Russia’s supposed planning for the coming months, nor would they comment on whether a surprise trip by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to Moscow last month – during which he stopped off in Riga – was partly to warn the Kremlin about the dangers of launching an attack on Nato.
After that visit, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed rumours of a Russian attack on Nato. “It has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation,” he said.
However, many in Europe will have the build up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in the back of their minds, when US officials repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invade and the Kremlin repeatedly denied it.
As the full-scale war that ensued approaches its fifth winter, US-led efforts to bring about peace in Ukraine show no signs of success, with Russia and Ukraine intensifying their drone and missile strikes on each other. Ukraine has destroyed much of Russia’s oil infrastructure, targeting refineries and other facilities over recent months.
Moscow has frequently said the provision to Ukraine of weaponry, intelligence and military advisers makes western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets, but has so far avoided action that might provoke a coordinated response from Nato. Instead, it has launched what western agencies describe as a campaign of sabotage against targets in countries that are the loudest backers of Ukraine, and one-off incidents apparently meant to test boundaries, such as when more than a dozen drones, flying without ammunition, veered into Polish airspace a year ago.
Koudelka said the current Russian tactic was “escalate to de-escalate”, with the Kremlin keen to push at weak points in western societies to tamp down their support for Ukraine’s war effort. “They believe if they escalate enough, then European countries will decide not to support Ukraine,” he said.
In recent weeks the Trump administration has made another attempt to kickstart peace negotiations in Ukraine. As well as the Ratcliffe visit to Moscow, the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made another trip to Moscow, as well as a first-time trip to Kyiv. While Donald Trump has frequently claimed the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, is interested in a deal, there is scepticism in Europe that the Kremlin has any interest in good-faith negotiations.
“I haven’t seen any signs that there is a serious consideration in Moscow about real negotiations,” said Thomas Nilsson, the head of Sweden’s military intelligence and security service, in an interview on the sidelines of a conference in Riga. “My assessment is that they are still thinking that they could achieve their strategic objectives, so they are just playing negotiation theatre,” he added.
All three intelligence bosses said that whatever else happened, Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe is likely to intensify in the coming months. Nilsson described as a “gamechanger” the recent armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, which German authorities have attributed to Russian intelligence.
“To have an armed UAV drone sent in to a busy airport in the middle of Europe … If you have attacks that could result in losses of life or losses of very critical infrastructure that have a huge implication for society, I think that is a gamechanger,” he said.
Mežviets said Russia was moving from randomised targeting of sabotage and arson attacks intended to sow panic to specific targets linked to western backing for Ukraine. “We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure. Right now we see a move towards defence industry targets,” he said. “If you do this then the psy-op effect is reached anyway, so you get both things in one,” he added.
Nilsson said there were several goals behind the recent intensification of Russian sabotage activity: to reduce support for Ukraine, to introduce splits in Nato and to alarm European populations. “I think Moscow would love Nato to have endless discussion about article 4 consultations, but coming up with no actions,” he said.
Koudelka said another effect of the sabotage campaign is the stretch on resources of intelligence services, as doubts often linger even when incidents are caused by other factors. “Now every fire or every malfunction needs to be investigated by intelligence services as a potential terror attack, and that is a good result for them,” he said.

articles.title: Hundreds of drones target Moscow on last day of voting in Russia’s parliamentary election
articles.body:
Ukraine has targeted Moscow and the surrounding region in a large-scale attack that involved hundreds of drones.
The attack killed at least three people and damaged what Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said was one of Russia’s “key oil industry facilities” on the final day of the country’s parliamentary elections, authorities said on Sunday.
Zelenskyy said that among the weapons used in the attack was the Pelican, initially thought to be a short-range ballistic missile, but which sources said later was a winged drone.
The president did not offer any further details, prompting media reports in Ukraine that it was a ballistic missile, only for doubt to be cast on the weapon identification later in the day.
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine had used its domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles to strike Moscow. The long-range weapon has previously been used against targets deep inside Russia and has the range to reach the country’s capital.
Ukrainian and Russian Telegram channels posted images of what they said was debris from a Flamingo missile found in the Moscow region, though the claims could not be independently verified. Ruslan Leviev, the head of the open-source investigation group Conflict Intelligence Team, said the debris probably came from a Flamingo missile.
Moscow’s mayor, Sergey Sobyanin, said that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted and shot down, 450 of which were aimed at Moscow, though these figures are often exaggerated, and Ukraine’s daily drone fire rate estimated a number in the low hundreds.
Sobyanin accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with a tightly controlled three-day election in Russia that is expected to tighten Vladimir Putin’s 26-year grip on power.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram.
At least three people were killed, including a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man, in separate incidents.
A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building also led to 400 people being evacuated, said Moscow’s regional governor, Andrey Vorobyov, without specifying the drone’s origin.
Kyiv has stepped up its campaign of long-range drone strikes against Russia in recent months, particularly against energy infrastructure, a vital source of the Kremlin’s revenue to fund its war effort.
Ukrainian strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia’s oil-refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country’s 11 time zones.
A facility on the territory of the Moscow oil refinery had been damaged, Sobyanin said. No casualties were reported and emergency services were on the scene. The refinery had already been hit by Ukrainian strikes in recent months.
The Pelican missile was initially thought to be the FP-7 made by Fire Point, Ukraine’s most successful long-range drone and missile maker. But several hours later, as the speculation persisted, other military sources said it was a long-range drone.
The company is also developing the longer-range FP-9, which has a range of more than 500 miles, meaning it could be used to target Moscow in the future. A test flight is expected later this autumn.
The latest strike comes after the US president, Donald Trump, said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities. It also comes after Russians began voting on Friday in the country’s first parliamentary elections since Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine. Few Russians doubt Putin’s United Russia party will coast to victory again, but the vote offers a gauge of public support for the war.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: MP: US criminal act in Lamerd and Minab is a modern example of crimes in Hiroshima and Nagasa
articles.body:
MP: US criminal act in Lamerd and Minab is a modern example of crimes in Hiroshima and Nagasa
TEHRAN — Iran’s Deputy Parliament Speaker Hamid Reza Haji Babaei has lashed out at the United States over its deadly strikes against civilian targets in southern Iran, declaring Washington’s strikes on the city of Lamerd and the Shajareh Tayyebah school in Minab as direct modern manifestations of the atomic atrocities perpetrated against Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
Speaking during an open parliamentary session on Sunday, Haji Babaei reiterated Tehran’s resolve to hold the United States legally and politically accountable for blatant violations of international law and international humanitarian statutes.
“The criminal action of the United States in Lamerd and the Shajareh Tayyebah school in Minab is a textbook example of modern-day crimes akin to what transpired in Hiroshima and Nagasaki,” Haji Babaei said in response to a parliamentary notice raised by Musa Mousavi, the lawmaker representing Lamerd and Mohr.
“This is the exact same course of savagery, merely updated with modern technology and weapon systems. It demonstrates that the US continues to expand its repertoire of war crimes and brutality against sovereign nations while brazenly trampling basic human values,” the deputy speaker emphasized.
During his address on the Majlis floor, Musa Mousavi detailed the horrific dimensions of the strike on Lamerd, characterizing it as an indisputable war crime aimed deliberately at maximizing human suffering.
According to Mousavi, four precision-guided ballistic missiles—identified as Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM)—were fired into Lamerd, tearing through two residential neighborhoods and a public indoor sports arena.
Mousavi explained that the munitions deployed in Lamerd were designed specifically for wide-area lethality rather than standard structural demolition. Instead of detonating upon ground impact, the warheads exploded roughly 40 meters in the air, releasing an indiscriminate hail of 180,000 tungsten fragments per missile over a 360-degree radius.
“In total, 720,000 tungsten pellets were rained down on Lamerd. In a city of 30,000 people, this amounts to an average of 24 lethal projectiles for every single resident,” Mousavi noted, presenting photographs of perforated walls, doors, and residential infrastructure pockmarked with hundreds of shrapnel holes.
The lawmaker underscored that several factors prevented a significantly larger catastrophe beyond the recorded toll of 21 martyrs and 60 injured: the attack struck near the evening Iftar when families were indoors, the residential zones were less congested, and a neighboring school complex was empty at that hour.
Mousavi slammed the provocative rhetoric from US military commanders who praised the deployment of these weapons to “put pressure on the Iranian populace,” while highlighting how arms contractors such as Lockheed Martin subsequently saw inflated multibillion-dollar procurement contracts.
Echoing the directives of the Leader—who instructed the Iranian Judiciary to vigorously pursue legal cases against the United States over the carnage in Lamerd and Minab—Mousavi called on Iranian diplomats to turn these strikes into an international indictment against Washington across multilateral bodies.
The attacks on Lamerd and Minab represent some of the most devastating strikes on civilian infrastructure in southern Iran, sparking worldwide outrage and international scrutiny over Washington’s unlawful targeting methodologies.
The Tragedy of Shajareh Tayyebah
 
 Located in the eastern coastal plain of Hormozgan Province near the Strait of Hormuz, Minab is an ancient agricultural and trade hub, home to roughly 75,000 residents.
On February 28, the civilian population of Minab suffered one of the deadliest single mass-casualty attacks when a US cruise missile pulverized the Shajareh Tayyebah Elementary School during morning classes. The strike brought down the multi-story educational facility, martyring nearly 170 civilians—the vast majority of them young schoolchildren.
Independent investigations and a formal report by the United Nations Fact-Finding Mission concluded that the strike constituted an indiscriminate attack and a potential war crime. Inquiries revealed that US forces had relied on decades-old, obsolete intelligence regarding a nearby historical installation, failing to take basic precautions to verify the presence of active educational institutions.
Lamerd, situated in the southernmost tip of Fars Province near the Persian Gulf energy corridor, is a strategic hub of energy, aluminum manufacturing, and commerce. Bordering Bushehr and Hormozgan, the county sits atop major natural gas fields, including the Tabnak and Eram reservoirs, and hosts the sprawling Lamerd Special Economic Zone (housing the South Aluminum Corporation, SALCO).
Despite its purely civilian and economic profile, residential districts and civic sports infrastructure inside Lamerd were subjected to air-burst tungsten fragmentation strikes. Rather than striking isolated strategic installations, the deployment of anti-personnel fragmentation warheads over residential quarters underscored a calculated attempt to inflict maximum civilian terror.

articles.title: US envoy highlights AI rivalry with China, warns against domestic innovation caps
articles.body:
Yasin Gungor
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
The US faces a more complex challenge from China in competing for artificial intelligence (AI) than it did during the Cold War, when the two countries had fewer economic ties, US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said Sunday.
"Unlike in the Cold War or any other adversary we've had in the past—Germany, Japan, etc.—we've never been so intertwined economically with a competitor or potential adversary like we are with the People's Republic of China, so it is a much more complex situation," Waltz told US television network CNN.
Waltz indicated that Washington sees space for narrow bilateral guardrails during an upcoming summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, pointing to rules regarding algorithmic diffusion, nuclear weapons systems, and keeping humans in command loops.
However, he drew a firm line against domestic regulatory limits. "What we cannot do is put a throttle on our innovators, on our entrepreneurs, on so many great Americans in our system that's so unique that are creating the solutions of the future," Waltz said.
Arctic security and polar trade corridors
Addressing northern defense, Waltz framed a new security agreement between the US and Denmark over Greenland as an urgent requirement for strategic early warning.
"If we're ever attacked by any type of intercontinental missiles, they'll come over the Arctic," Waltz explained, stressing that radar and sensor installations in the region require robust protection and unrestricted access.
The envoy connected northern access to continental missile defense systems, an icebreaker pact reached with Finland, expanded military spending within NATO, and resource extraction across polar energy and critical mineral reserves.
He noted that retreating ice leads shipping to bypass southern chokepoints and traverse Arctic routes, making diplomatic pacts with Denmark and Greenland essential to safeguarding the High North.
Maritime defense and Iran war pressure
Turning to Middle Eastern waterways, Waltz said the US and its allies will take "decisive action" against any actors disrupting civilian maritime traffic across the Bab al-Mandeb, Strait of Hormuz, and Suez Canal.
Responding to reports that military confrontations could stretch toward 2029, Waltz said time favors Washington.
He explained that sanctions will remain indefinite until verified nuclear and behavioral concessions take place, claiming that the pressure directly targets Tehran's power structure because the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) controls 40% to 50% of the Iranian economy.
Meanwhile, CNN reported that the Trump administration prefers that Saudi Arabia counter the push rather than using American force directly.
A US official told the network that Washington is expanding targeting data and intelligence sharing with Riyadh, while sources noted Saudi officials expressed confidence in their forces following a decade of training.

articles.title: Ukraine Intel Tests Remote-Controlled Quad Bikes for Front Line
articles.body:
Special operators from the Main Directorate of Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR) have conducted closed-door field trials of domestically manufactured quad bikes, focusing on platforms equipped with remote-control capabilities, the state defense technology cluster Brave1 reported.
The operational testing was carried out by combat operators from the 33 Group, a specialized detachment within the HUR’s Tymur Special Operations Unit. The reconnaissance personnel operated the vehicles directly across simulated tactical scenarios to evaluate handling, endurance, and field reliability, providing engineers with immediate technical feedback for modifications.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Brave1 stated that the evaluation was structured around operational criteria vital for autumn and winter frontline deployments, where unpaved terrain, mud, and intense drone surveillance complicate standard logistical operations.
The military requires versatile platforms that can transition between conventional driver operation and remote control to transport supplies, evacuate casualties, and conduct tactical resupply across contested sectors without exposing operators to direct enemy observation.
While the Armed Forces of Ukraine utilize foreign-manufactured all-terrain vehicles, cluster representatives noted that imported models carry high acquisition costs and lack organic remote-piloting capabilities. To address the gap, Brave1 has integrated unmanned quad bikes into a targeted grant program intended to foster an indigenous production ecosystem.
Russian Drone Strikes Ukrposhta Mobile Branch in Sumy
“Our goal is to build a fully-fledged Ukrainian buggy market,” Brave1 said, noting that the cluster has provided financial grants to developers representing more than half of the buggy designs currently operating domestically.
Following the trials, manufacturers began refining transmission, communications links, and control software based on operator assessments. The defense-tech cluster noted that subsequent phases will involve coordination with the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine to codify the vehicles and scale serial procurement for frontline units.
Scaling domestic defense tech and indigenous munitions
The development of automated all-terrain vehicles forms part of a broader drive by Ukraine’s defense-industrial base and the Brave1 innovation cluster to field cost-effective, indigenously designed military hardware to counter Russian numerical superiority.
The initiative follows the unveiling in early September of the RK-19, a domestically produced surface-to-air missile engineered to replace dwindling Soviet-era munitions for Ukraine’s Osa-AKM mobile air defense systems.
The RK-19 missile, developed by Ukrainian state defense enterprises and showcased at the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland, was designed to substitute for Soviet 9M33-series interceptors.
The missile is engineered to intercept low-altitude aerial targets at distances of up to 10 kilometers and altitudes reaching 5 kilometers, reaching a maximum speed of 600 meters per second using radio-command guidance.
Ukrainian defense planners have accelerated domestic substitution programs as international munitions deliveries fluctuate and existing Soviet stockpiles approach exhaustion.
In late summer, Ukrainian officials noted that deliveries of foreign air defense missiles had fallen threefold compared with 2025 levels, prompting domestic developers to prioritize cost-effective interceptors and decentralized tactical platforms.
Brave1 developers have also introduced asymmetric countermeasures against high-speed aerial threats, demonstrating low-cost interception technologies designed to counter Russian loitering munitions and hybrid drone-missiles at a fraction of the cost of conventional anti-aircraft missiles.
