articles.title: ‘Russophobic West’ to blame for lost Ukraine peace chance – NATO state leader
articles.body:
‘Russophobic West’ to blame for lost Ukraine peace chance – NATO state leader
Ukraine made a “huge mistake” by caving in to its Western backers and walking away from a potential peace deal with Russia in 2022, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said. He also argued that years of Western military backing have failed to defeat Russia and are now raising the risk of a direct clash between Russia and NATO.
In a video address posted on X on Saturday, Fico argued that both sides have sustained “terrible” losses over the years, and that Western military support has failed to contain Russia’s advances. “There is no supranational force to compel Russia to withdraw from the militarily controlled Ukrainian territory,” he said.
“Ukraine made a huge mistake in April 2022, a few months after the start of the conflict, by listening to the Russophobic West and not signing the prepared peace agreement,” he said, adding that the Western strategy “to support the war in Ukraine to the last Ukrainian soldier and defeat Russia” has “completely failed.” He reiterated that his government will not provide military assistance or loans to Ukraine.
Confronted with the failure to destroy Russia through the Ukraine conflict, “several politicians in the West… believe that if it cannot be achieved through the Ukrainian army and its full support, everything must be done to provoke a conflict between NATO and Russia,” Fico stated.
“Someone must have gone crazy here,” he said, arguing that “Russia cannot be defeated in a conventional war” and noting that it has a vast nuclear arsenal.
Fico stressed that the Ukraine conflict is “not a NATO war,” arguing that “only some war hawks in NATO are trying at all costs to turn this war into a conflict between Russia and NATO.”
He noted that the Slovaks had their own experience with the Munich Agreement in 1938, saying that “the powers bound to us by treaty deceived us, betrayed us, and served us up to Hitler like a roasted chicken.” The Munich Accord – which was a prelude to World War II – was signed by Nazi Germany, Britain, France, and Italy without Czechoslovakia at the table and compelled Prague to surrender the predominantly German-speaking Sudetenland.
In spring 2022, Russia and Ukraine made substantial progress toward a peace deal, including a tentative draft agreement on Ukrainian neutrality, security guarantees, and other core issues.
Russia accused then-UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson of helping derail the peace process, which he has denied. Ukrainian chief negotiator David Arakhamia later confirmed that Johnson played an influential role. He said Russia was prepared to end the conflict if Kiev accepted neutrality, adding that Johnson told Ukrainian officials, “We won’t sign anything with them at all, and let’s just fight.”
While the peace settlement process intensified after US President Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, no breakthroughs have been achieved. In February, the Russian Defense Ministry said Ukrainian military casualties exceeded 1.5 million since 2022, including more than 520,000 in 2025 alone.

articles.title: New US sanctions law undermines Ukraine peace efforts – Kremlin
articles.body:
New US sanctions law undermines Ukraine peace efforts – Kremlin
The sanctions law signed by US President Donald Trump this week will undermine efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict through diplomacy, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
On Friday, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which authorizes tougher restrictions on Russia and tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
“Clearly, this cannot have a positive effect,” Peskov told RIA Novosti on Saturday when asked how the law would affect the prospects for a peaceful settlement in Ukraine and the possibility of a breakthrough in Russia-US relations.
Named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who co-authored the original bill with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal in 2025, the legislation remained stalled for months as Trump pursued diplomacy with Russia and resisted placing sole blame for the conflict on Moscow. Trump’s envoys also discussed normalizing economic ties with their Russian counterparts.
The Senate passed the measure 86-11 last month, followed by the House on Wednesday in a 262-159 vote.
The original proposal threatened tariffs of 500% on countries purchasing Russian energy, but the maximum rate was reduced to 100% after negotiations with the White House. Graham, who died unexpectedly in July, promoted the measure as “bone-crushing” sanctions.
The version adopted by Congress targets major buyers of Russian oil and gas, with China and India expected to be among those potentially affected. It also gives Trump broad discretion over the application of the tariffs, including the ability to waive or suspend restrictions in the national interest.
Peskov previously described the bill as an “unfriendly action” that would “complicate efforts to find a peaceful settlement in Ukraine.”
The Russian Embassy in the US said the legislation does “a grand disservice” to Trump’s ‘Make America Great Again’ agenda, arguing that restricting Russia’s energy trade amid sharply reduced Middle Eastern supplies could send fuel prices soaring ahead of the midterm elections. It warned that confrontation with Russia and China is a lose-lose situation that only benefits the “Euro-Atlantic warmongers.”
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun condemned the law, saying China “carries out economic and trade cooperation with countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit” and that its trade is not directed against any third country.

articles.body:
Türkiye has revoked the license of Iran’s Bank Mellat, a semi-private financial entity that has been subject to Western sanctions for years, the Official Gazette said early on Sept. 19.
The decision was announced some two weeks after Washington slapped sanctions on a Turkish bank over alleged ties to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) although it was not immediately clear whether the two issues were related.
The move follows a decision by Türkiye’s banking regulator over the Tehran-based bank, which provides financial support to Iran’s government and is subject to U.S., EU and U.K. sanctions, according to
OpenSanctions, an open-source database of information on sanctions-hit entities.
The Iranian government is also the largest shareholder of the bank, it said.
In revoking Bank Mellat’s license, the Turkish regulator cited article 71b of the banking law, which says the entity’s “continued operation poses a threat to the rights of depositors and participation fund holders and to the security and stability of the financial system.”
Bank Mellat has been subjected to Western sanctions for years over accusations that Tehran was pursuing an atomic weapon under the cover of a civil nuclear program.
On Sept. 4, the U.S. Treasury Department imposed sanctions on Türkiye’s Golden Global Bank over its alleged ties to the Revolutionary Guards as it sought to step up financial pressure on Iran.
The Turkish investment bank denied the accusations.
A few days later, Washington imposed sanctions on 36 entities, including three Turkish ground services companies, for helping Iran’s Mahan Air, a civilian carrier accused of supporting the Revolutionary Guards.
Following the move, Mahan Air said this week it would suspend all flights to Türkiye from Sept. 21 at the request of Turkish aviation authorities, Iran’s ISNA news agency reported.
Iran has been at war since late February, when the United States and Israel launched a surprise bombing campaign that killed the Islamic republic’s supreme leader.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said Washington was declaring an “economic D-Day” on Iran, warning of harsh consequences for countries that do not join the campaign.

articles.title: Pahlavi: Iran regime continues to erode from within as defections grow
articles.body:
Iran’s exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi said Saturday that members of the Islamic Republic’s military and civilian establishment were already quietly breaking with the regime, describing Iran as having entered an “active defection” phase in the struggle to overthrow the country’s rulers.
Addressing thousands of supporters at the "Cyrus the Great II" gathering in Toronto over the weekend, Pahlavi outlined how in the months since the bloody January uprising, when over 40,000 Iranians were killed on the streets, the opposition had regrouped, adapted its tactics and expanded networks inside Iran, even as the regime sought to convince Iranians that the protest movement had been defeated.
“We are more experienced, more cohesive and more determined today than ever before,” he told the gathering. “Our objective is clear: the overthrow of the Islamic Republic and achieving a free and prosperous Iran.”
Central to his speech was the claim that erosion within the regime itself is continuing. For months, Pahlavi has said that officials from within the Islamic Republic’s apparatus have been quietly reaching out to him to signal their clandestine opposition to the regime.
These members of Iran’s civilian and military structures have used secure channels to distance themselves from the Islamic Republic and side with the opposition. For now, Pahlavi argued, many remain outwardly within the system, retaining their positions while gradually ceasing to perform the functions expected of them.
“They remain within the structure outwardly, but they no longer perform their former functions for the regime,” he said. “Quietly, but decisively, they are eroding the pillars of repression from within.”
Open defections, including soldiers publicly laying down their weapons, would represent a later stage reached once the balance of power had shifted decisively toward the opposition.
Pahlavi placed January's anti-regime protests within cycle of longer period of Iran unrest
During his Toronto address, Pahlavi also placed January’s uprising within a much longer period of unrest in Iran, dating back through several protest cycles.
Rather than portraying December-January’s demonstrations as an isolated explosion of anger, he traced their origins through a decade of growing opposition, from the large Cyrus Day gatherings of 2016, through the protests of 2017-18 and November 2019, to the nationwide uprising that followed Mahsa Amini's death in 2022. Saturday also saw global marches across the Iranian diaspora to mark four years since Amini’s death in the custody of the Iranian regime.
“The great uprising of Dey was not the product of a fleeting burst of emotion,” he said. “Behind it lay a long, difficult and costly road.”
The events of January 8 and 9, when the Islamic Republic launched a massive crackdown as demonstrations spread across the country, had nevertheless changed the circumstances confronting the opposition.
The scale of the killing, Pahlavi said, required changes in how the opposition operated, although not in what it ultimately sought to achieve.
“A change in tactics does not mean a change in objectives. It means adapting our methods to new circumstances.”
Saturday’s gathering was held at Meridian Hall as part of "Cyrus the Great II: From a Great Civilization to a Greater Future," organized by the Cyrus the Great Cultural & Humanity Organization. Organizers had said ahead of the event that more than 3,000 Iranian Canadians and supporters were expected.
The event brought Pahlavi together with Canadian political and civic figures, most prominently Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre, who used his appearance to call for stronger Canadian action against individuals linked to the Islamic Republic.
Canada's Poilievre calls for scrutiny on IRGC-linked actors entering country
Poilievre called for greater scrutiny of those connected to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps entering Canada, continued targeted sanctions, and measures to prevent regime-linked assets from being moved into the country.
Canada severed diplomatic relations with Tehran in 2012 and designated the IRGC as a terrorist entity in 2024.
Poilievre also spoke of Iran beyond the Islamic Republic, invoking Cyrus the Great and the country’s pre-Islamic history while expressing hope that Iranians would one day be able to return freely to their country and see the Lion and Sun flag raised there again.
For Pahlavi, much of Saturday’s address focused on another battle between the opposition and Tehran: the competing picture each presents of the state of resistance inside Iran. He accused the regime of promoting two central claims – that Iran’s opposition remains hopelessly divided and that no meaningful organization exists inside the country.
On the first, Pahlavi argued that agreement over Iran’s eventual form of government was not a prerequisite for cooperation against the Islamic Republic.
Republicans and monarchists, as well as those on the political left and right, could work together around four principles: Iran’s territorial integrity; separation of religion and government; individual freedoms and equality before the law; and Iranians' right to determine their future system of government through free and fair elections.
“The embrace of Iran’s Lion and Sun Revolution is open to every Iranian who accepts these four principles,” he said.
The second claim – that the opposition lacks organization – brought Pahlavi back to the networks he says now operate beneath the surface inside Iran.
If no organization existed, he asked, how could millions of Iranians inside and outside the country act together at critical moments?
According to Pahlavi, the answer lies in decentralized networks embedded in Iranian society, beyond the regime’s ability to easily dismantle. He claimed Tehran’s intelligence and security apparatus was itself increasingly concerned by their development.
The Iranian opposition leader nevertheless cautioned his supporters against assuming the Islamic Republic’s collapse was inevitable or imminent.
“We must be realistic. The work is not yet finished,” he said. “Overthrowing this criminal sect that has occupied our country is a complex, multi-stage process.”
But the central message of the Toronto speech was that Pahlavi believes that process has moved into a different stage – one increasingly focused on weakening the machinery of the Islamic Republic from within.
“The enemy is decaying from within and is hollow,” he told the crowd. “We are more determined and more organized than ever. Believe that the dawn of freedom is near.”

articles.title: South Korea, US discuss Seoul's role in Middle East, investment pact
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
South Korea, US discuss Seoul's role in Middle East, investment pact
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday as the longtime allies grappled with delayed Korean investments in the United States and Seoul's role in Middle East security.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Seoul in recent weeks over what he described as a lack of South Korean support for US efforts to pressure Iran. The two countries have also yet to finalise agreements governing $350 billion in South Korean investments pledged under a trade deal reached last year.
Cho explained to Rubio Seoul's willingness to make a substantive contribution to restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, the ministry said in a statement without elaborating.
On Seoul's investment commitments, Rubio stressed their swift execution, the State Department said, while South Korea's foreign ministry said Rubio and Cho agreed to keep communicating to ensure ongoing consultation plans "bear good fruit".
Rubio and Cho also pledged ongoing collaboration across key strategic sectors including semiconductors, the State Department said, while Rubio underscored the need for a fair and transparent business environment for US companies in South Korea.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who is due in the United States next week for the UN General Assembly, said on Friday he would not deploy military assets to the Middle East in a way that could draw the country into conflict.
However, he said Seoul was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region.
Cho said before leaving Seoul on Thursday that investment plans under its trade deal had been delayed while procedural issues were clarified, without elaborating.
Lee told a news conference on Friday that concerns over the commercial viability of the package had become a sticking point in negotiations, although the two sides were nearing an agreement.
He said some elements of the package were difficult for Seoul to accept, but the government would continue discussions to ensure any deal protects South Korea's interests while benefiting both countries and the broader US-South Korea relationship.
Seoul committed last year to invest in US manufacturing in return for lowering tariffs on imports from South Korean to 15%.
Lee said Seoul had insisted on including a reference to "commercially reasonable" investments in the text of the agreement.
North Korea also featured in the talks, amid speculation over a possible summit between Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Rubio and Cho reaffirmed their commitment to the complete denuclearization of North Korea, the State Department said, while Cho said Seoul would actively support the resumption of talks between Washington and Pyongyang, according to the ministry.
President Lee said on Friday it was possible for a summit meeting between Kim and Trump to take place in coming months, but it remained uncertain.

articles.title: French facilities that could face Russian hybrid attacks identified
articles.body:
French facilities that could face Russian hybrid attacks identified
France is preparing for Russian hybrid attacks targeting its infrastructure, which could take place as early as autumn 2027.
Source: French media outlet Franceinfo, as reported by European Pravda
Details: On 18 September, French President Emmanuel Macron met with the leaders of all political parties, including candidates in the 2027 presidential election.
The meeting took place in the Élysée Palace's new crisis room, which has the highest level of security. Macron reportedly sought to warn presidential candidates about potential Russian attacks.
According to a confidential memo obtained by France Télévisions, several infrastructure facilities are mentioned as potential Russian targets, including power plants and electricity grids, railways, telecommunications networks and drinking water distribution systems.
"It should be known that French airfields, of course, the main ones, are protected against attacks or drone incursions. But one can imagine that all important facilities linked to defence could become targets," said General Patrick Dutartre of the French Air and Space Force.
French intelligence services are preparing for large-scale Russian attacks by 2030. However, according to France Télévisions, the timeframe is now autumn 2027.
Faced with a threat of unprecedented scale, the French government has taken unprecedented measures and convened an emergency meeting of all prefects. As early as next week, they are due to establish security and defence headquarters in their departments. Local law enforcement and military leaders, representatives of the Ministry of Education, business executives and emergency responders will take part in the discussions.
Following the meeting with political party leaders on 18 September, Macron highlighted the growing Russian hybrid threat and ordered the preparation of a plan to protect critical infrastructure against it.
"I have asked the government to prepare a plan to protect our critical infrastructure, as well as the most vulnerable facilities in our defence industrial and technological base, from drone and cyberattacks," the French president said.
Background:
- In a statement released on 19 September, two leading figures of France's far-right National Rally, Marine Le Pen, the leading presidential candidate, and Jordan Bardella, took a firm position towards Moscow.
- Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, citing intelligence data, that Russia is planning hybrid attacks against countries supporting Ukraine.

articles.title: Two civilians killed as Ukrainian drones strike homes near Moscow
articles.body:
Russia downs 1,600 Ukrainian drones in ‘unprecedented’ attack during elections – Moscow mayor
Two civilians were killed and several others, including two children, were injured in Moscow Region during a powerful Ukrainian drone raid that was aimed at derailing Russia’s parliamentary elections, local officials said.
In a statement on Sunday, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said more than 1,600 UAVs were repelled since the previous day, adding that 450 UAVs were intercepted on approaches to the capital.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned to disrupt the elections. The enemy failed,” he said.
Several drones reached the premises of the Moscow Oil Refinery, where one unidentified facility was damaged, and one struck a residential building, according to Sobyanin, who said there were no fatalities in the capital.
The consequences of the raid, however, were much more destructive in the suburbs. Earlier in the day, Moscow Region Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported damage in the Ramenskoye District, southeast of Moscow, where a 44-year-old woman was killed and five others, including two children, were injured when a drone hit an apartment building in the village of Sofyino.
In the nearby city of Ramenskoye, around 400 people, including 70 children, were evacuated from a 21-story apartment block after falling drone debris sparked a fire on the roof, with 20 vehicles also damaged.
Another person was killed in the Orekhovo-Zuyevo District, where a private home was destroyed and caught fire during the attack. The victim was an elderly man who was inside the building, according to the governor.
Elsewhere in Moscow Region, a warehouse complex caught fire in Sofyino, and a drone struck an apartment building in Kotelniki, setting apartments on three floors ablaze. The authorities are still determining whether anyone was injured.
Private homes were also damaged in Kolomna and Yegoryevsk, while fires broke out at apartment buildings in the Leninsky District, Lyubertsy, and Lytkarino. A residential building and an industrial facility were damaged in Istra, with no casualties reported.
The massive raid struck Moscow and the surrounding region just hours before polling stations were due to open for the final day of Russia’s three-day parliamentary elections. Despite the attack, all 1,443 polling stations in Moscow opened on time, Moscow Election Commission Deputy Chairman Dmitry Reut told TASS.
Moscow has accused Kiev of undermining diplomatic efforts while publicly calling for renewed negotiations. On Friday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said the Ukrainian leadership is “talking about peace” while doing everything to prevent peace and negotiations.
Earlier this month, Putin ordered large-scale retaliatory strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in response to attacks inside Russia. Moscow has condemned the strikes on civilians as acts of terrorism, while maintaining that Russian forces only target military and defense-related facilities.

articles.title: China slams ‘unilateral’ US sanctions law targeting Russia, Iran
articles.body:
China slams ‘unilateral’ US sanctions law targeting Russia, Iran
TEHRAN – The Chinese Ministry of Commerce has issued a sharp rebuke against Washington’s latest legislative maneuvers, condemning the newly enacted US law that seeks to tighten sanctions on Russia and broaden trade restrictions against Iran.
The legislation, signed by President Donald Trump late Friday, has been met with immediate disapproval from Beijing. A spokesperson for China’s Commerce Ministry stated on Saturday that China has “consistently opposed” the implementation of unilateral sanctions and the extraterritorial application of secondary sanctions, which critics argue violate the foundational principles of international relations.
In a formal statement, the spokesperson underscored that Beijing remains firmly against any coercive economic measures that lack authorization from the United Nations or any grounding in established international law.
The US law, which authorizes the imposition of tariffs on nations purchasing Russian petroleum products, has drawn scrutiny for its potential to destabilize global energy markets and disrupt diplomatic efforts. The measure, viewed by observers as a thinly veiled tool of economic warfare, threatens to impact several major economies, including China, India, and Turkey, as well as several European Union member states that continue to engage in energy trade with Russia.
“China will closely monitor Washington’s next steps,” the spokesperson said, emphasizing that Beijing “reserves the right to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty, development interests, and the legitimate rights and interests of its companies.”
Analysts observe that this latest aggressive move by the White House marks yet another chapter in Washington’s deteriorating approach to global diplomacy. By weaponizing the global financial system and dictating the economic policies of sovereign nations, the United States is further eroding the trust of its own allies and isolating itself from the emerging multipolar order.
Critics argue that such measures are not aimed at fostering international security, but are instead designed to maintain American hegemony at the expense of global economic stability. By targeting independent nations like Iran—a key partner in China’s global development initiatives—the US is signaling an intensified effort to obstruct the sovereign economic development of the Global South.
The statement further reiterated China’s commitment to the stability of global trade, urging the United States to abandon its policy of economic coercion in favor of dialogue and mutual consultation.
As Washington continues to utilize its domestic legislation to project power globally, Beijing’s response signals a hardening stance against what many international observers describe as an increasingly erratic and unilateralist US foreign policy.

articles.title: EU facing ‘worst energy crisis in history’ – Putin envoy
articles.body:
EU facing ‘worst energy crisis in history’ – Putin envoy
Europe is facing “the worst energy crisis in history,” Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev has warned, describing the situation as a “self-made.” He has repeatedly blamed the EU’s decision to cut Russian energy imports as a key factor behind the crisis.
Dmitriev made the remarks after reports of worsening fuel shortages across the EU. Government data on Sunday showed that 15% of French gas stations were facing supply problems with at least one type of petrol or diesel.
German media also reported record fuel prices, with Super E10 gasoline reaching around €2.3 ($2.6) per liter and diesel averaging a record €2.45. Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% higher than a year ago, diesel is up 38%, and jet fuel costs more than double. Benchmark gas prices have surged 150% year-on-year to €81 per megawatt hour, with analysts warning they could reach €100.
“Europe finally understands it is facing the worst energy crisis in history,” Dmitriev wrote in a series of posts on X on Saturday, calling it “a self-made crisis with zero attempts to analyze root causes and adjust course.”
Self-made crisis with zero attempts to analyze root causes and adjust course. https://t.co/zvdb0RkYsE
— Kirill Dmitriev (@kadmitriev) September 20, 2026
The bloc this year has faced mounting supply pressures from the US-Israeli war on Iran, which disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and LNG.
Combined with Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping and Saudi energy infrastructure, the disruptions pushed crude benchmarks up around 50%, with prices hovering above $100 per barrel and driving fuel and gas costs higher. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen this week said the EU had spent more than €90 billion extra on fossil fuel imports since the war began. Much of the additional expense was passed on to households. Brussels also previously acknowledged that industrial gas and electricity prices remain two to four times higher than those of major trading partners.
The Middle East conflict, however, has further pressured energy markets already strained by Europe’s sharp reduction in Russian supplies following sanctions imposed after the 2022 escalation of the Ukraine conflict. Before then, Russia supplied around 45% of EU gas imports and 27% of crude oil. By 2025, its share had fallen to 12% of gas imports and around 2% of crude.
Even sanctions supporters, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, have linked Europe’s energy challenges to the loss of cheap Russian supplies. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned earlier this month that the EU cannot remain competitive while energy costs stay prohibitively high.
Meanwhile, the EU is entering the heating season with its lowest gas storage levels in 15 years. According to Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE), underground facilities were just 69.3% as of Saturday, below the 85% average for this time of the year over the last five years, prompting warnings of heightened price volatility and higher energy bills this winter.
Despite the dire situation, von der Leyen reaffirmed in her State of the Union address this week that the EU will continue with its REPowerEU plan to permanently end reliance on Russian energy, with Russian LNG set to leave the EU market completely by the end of 2026 and pipeline gas by autumn 2027.
Moscow has long criticized Western energy sanctions as illegal and counterproductive, arguing they have redirected Russian exports while forcing Europe toward more expensive supplies. Russia has offered to help fill oil shortages caused by the Middle East conflict and resume energy deliveries but says it has received no response. Earlier this year, Dmitriev said the EU would “inevitably beg” for Russian gas as energy prices continue rising.

articles.title: US issues security alerts across Middle East
articles.body:
US issues security alerts across Middle East
The US has issued security alerts for its citizens across the Middle East, warning of further escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.
The notices cover Israel, Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, and Oman.
“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” the US State Department said on Saturday night.
“Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports. This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly,” the notice read, urging Americans to refrain from traveling to the Middle East.
“Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including U.S. businesses and other institutions.”
The alert came amid anticipation of potential new US strikes on Iran or Houthi targets in Yemen, as Saudi Arabia reportedly sought assistance in repelling the militant group’s offensive against forces of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
Axios reporter Barak Ravid said US President Donald Trump cut his weekend stay at Camp David short and will return to the White House on Saturday evening, one day earlier than planned.
CNN national security analyst Alex Plitsas cited sources as saying that Trump held a meeting at Camp David to “deliberate and review Yemen strike options.” ABC News previously reported, citing US officials, that Washington would limit its involvement to providing intelligence and targeting assistance to Saudi Arabia.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have expanded the territory they control in western Yemen, capturing the port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Saudi Arabia recently suspended operations on its East-West oil pipeline, also known as Petroline, after it was damaged in a drone attack that Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq. The pipeline carries crude oil from the kingdom’s eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis previously declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in response to what the group described as an illegal siege of the parts of Yemen under its control.
A Saudi-led coalition first intervened in the Yemeni civil war in 2015 after the Houthis captured the capital, Sanaa, the previous year. The current hostilities mark the biggest escalation in the conflict since the UN-brokered truce of 2022.

articles.title: AI ‘warning shots’ focus Beijing on national security risks
articles.body:
AFP Photo
While AI researchers in the United States fret over out-of-control superintelligence wiping out humanity, Chinese policymakers have until now been more focused on immediate risks, from deepfakes to child safety.
But the alarming hacking ability of top artificial intelligence models is leading Beijing to see the dangers in a new light, with the spy agency chief warning this week that the technology could jeopardize national security.
The potential vulnerability of Chinese mega-app WeChat was also revealed recently when a small team of programmers in California said it had used AI to build a cyberattack “worm” that, if unleashed, could easily compromise millions of WeChat accounts.
“There are more similarities than differences when it comes to AI safety issues” in China and the United States, said Kevin Xu, founder of U.S.-based technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital.
But unlike in America, these “don’t get litigated or go viral in public in China,” Xu told AFP.
Nevertheless, the cybersecurity impact of AI agent bots acting without human oversight “would rank very high among the Chinese government’s biggest concerns.”
As the topic grabs global headlines, the pressure is on for President Xi Jinping and U.S. counterpart Donald Trump to discuss tackling the AI threats to both countries at in-person talks on Sept. 24, despite their rivalry in the field.
Both powers are “developing a more realistic and shared understanding of these risks, thereby heightening the sense of urgency” to work together, Sun Chenghao of Tsinghua University’s Center for International Security and Strategy told AFP.
Cooperation on shared safety evaluations for AI models or alert systems when crises emerge might be undermined by the fierce competition, however.
“We’re leading China in AI, and frankly I want to keep it that way,” Trump said when asked about calls from top U.S. labs for a coordinated slowdown of their cutting-edge work.
Meanwhile, Sun said, “China is concerned that ‘security’ may be used as a tool to restrict its technological development.”
A stark warning of the existential threat posed by self-improving future AI systems, posted on Sept. 14 on X by a researcher resigning from U.S. startup Anthropic, has fueled debate worldwide over how the technology should be governed.
China is already actively regulating how it is used, such as by prohibiting the creation of an AI-generated avatar in someone’s likeness without their consent.
“Chinese AI policy focuses more on real, present-day harms to society and people,” said Brian Tse, CEO at Concordia AI, a Beijing-based consultancy focused on AI safety.
“Beijing treats AI as a general-purpose technology, not a ‘god-in-a-box,’” he said.
It sees it as “something closer to electricity or the automobile: Enormously beneficial for society and industry, but ultimately manageable through regulation,” Tse said.
He added that “recent AI capability jumps, high-profile incidents acting as ‘warning shots,’ and a worrying pace of AI development through automation” had all pushed the technology up the list of priorities.

articles.title: Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits Moscow on last day of Russian elections

articles.title: Ukraine pummels Moscow with drones on last day of Russian election
articles.body:
Ukraine pummels Moscow with drones on last day of Russian election
Two people were killed in the Moscow region and the Russian capital’s oil refinery was also struck
Ukraine launched what Moscow’s mayor called the biggest ever drone attack on the Russian capital on Sunday, in what he said was an unsuccessful attempt to disrupt the final day of a parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for Russia’s war in Ukraine.
The drone strikes killed two people in the Moscow region and two more in the Russian-held part of Ukraine’s Kherson region, including an election official, according to Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin and election authorities. A facility at Moscow’s oil refinery, which has been targeted before, was also damaged.
“The biggest attack by enemy drones has been repelled. Since yesterday, more than 1,600 drones have been shot down across all fronts. Of these, 450 were approaching Moscow,” Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said in a statement on Telegram.
One of the drones had struck a residential building, but none of its residents had lost their lives, he said.

articles.title: In a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it? | Steve Bloomfield
articles.body:
If all goes to plan, at some stage in the coming weeks 15 diplomats will emerge from a small sound-proofed room deep in the bowels of the United Nations headquarters in New York and announce the organisation’s next secretary-general.
The person they choose will face a combination of challenges unlike any that their predecessors have had to deal with. Two of the security council’s permanent members, the US and Russia, are engaged in wars of choice that have no end in sight. A UN commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, but the UN has effectively been reduced to the role of bystander, pushed out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. The climate crisis is creating a cascade of new humanitarian disasters, while every day now seems to bring a new security threat caused by the unregulated rise of AI.
All of this is happening in a world in which the very principles of the UN – multilateralism, a rules-based order and international law – are under threat.
Secretary-general elections have rarely been this consequential and conversations about who should win will dominate the sidelines of the UN general assembly this week and next, as world leaders gather for the annual summit.
The UN, and the world it speaks for, desperately needs a new leader who is both charismatic and competent. Yet the five permanent members of the security council – the US, UK, France, Russia and China – hold a veto. Anyone who wants the job will need the approval of Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and, most importantly, Trump.
It is not easy to argue you are best placed to save the UN when the man you need to persuade would rather it fails.
Three informal straw polls have taken place so far and no frontrunner has emerged, indeed opposition to the two leading candidates rose in last Friday’s vote. For the first time in the organisation’s 80-year history serious discussions are quietly taking place about what would happen if no secretary-general is chosen at all.
Ten years ago, the election of António Guterres of Portugal was widely welcomed as a shot in the arm for the UN after a decade of the low-energy leadership of the South Korean Ban Ki-moon. In his previous role as the UN’s refugee chief he had been an outspoken activist and had pledged to continue speaking up for the world’s most vulnerable people. Then, a month later, Trump took office as the US president.
Earlier this year, he announced the US’s withdrawal from 31 UN organisations, including the bodies responsible for dealing with climate change and women’s health, while in July his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced the administration’s desire to “dismantle” the international criminal court “brick by brick”. The abrupt closure of the US’s aid and development programme, USAID, led to deaths around the world.
Most controversially, the establishment of Trump’s Board of Peace sparked fears that it could be used to supplant the UN itself. The UN meanwhile is in the grip of a financial crisis, with Guterres warning during the summer that it faced “imminent financial collapse” due to unpaid dues, much of it owed by the US.
And yet, despite everything, the UN is still standing – and still matters. It is only the UN, through its Framework Convention on Climate Change, that manages to focus international attention on the greatest crisis the world is facing. Despite dramatic cuts in funding, there are still 11 peacekeeping missions staffed by more than 50,000 personnel in some of the most dangerous parts of the world. The UN’s office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs remains the best hope for negotiating access to deliver aid in war zones, including Sudan.
This year the general assembly passed two landmark resolutions: one recognising the transatlantic slave trade as a crime, another to adopt a new world map that correctly recognises Africa’s size.
We don’t know what the candidates think of these decisions, nor do we know where they stand on the war in Ukraine or what their stance is on Israel’s actions in Gaza. Despite the election’s importance – and despite the relatively recent transparency of “vision statements” and hustings – the candidates’ campaigns have been overwhelmingly cautious.
Part of the reason, of course, is that someone standing on an ambitious platform would stand no chance of getting the job.
UN experts believe there is a chance that the two current frontrunners, Guyana’s former foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Costa Rica’s ex vice-president Rebeca Grynspan, might become good secretary-generals. But no one is blown away by the choice on offer.
For Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband, both of whom will be in New York this week at the UN general assembly, there is a choice to be made. The UK is yet to express a preference, indeed the UK team at the UN is said to be unimpressed with all the candidates. So far, it’s understood, they have not voted in favour of anyone in the first three straw polls. The UK and France are both hoping another candidate will emerge.
Whether they will be any better is an open question. The New York Post reported in July that Trump wanted Fifa president Gianni Infantino to get the job. There is next to no chance that would happen, but European diplomats fear a Trump-backed dark horse – possibly one without a diplomatic background – may emerge in the coming weeks. This is, after all, the man who has outsourced his nation’s diplomacy to his son-in-law and a real estate investor. So far, Trump has said nothing in public, although that may change on Tuesday when he gives his speech at the general assembly. Or a social media post spat out at two in the morning could upend the race entirely.
The chances of the “Permanent Five” failing to agree on a name remain slim, but plans are already being drawn up in case the worst happens. Guterres may be asked to stay on, while another possibility is that a collection of senior UN officials is asked to serve in administrative roles until a candidate is found. Either way, it would leave the UN rudderless at a time it needs to be anything but.
No one is getting this job without Trump’s say so. But once the new general secretary is in office, the US president will have less sway on their actions. They will potentially serve for 10 years, eight of which will be without Trump in the White House.
But even without Trump, this will be an almost impossible job. The UN’s financial crisis is not going away. Severe cuts are coming. There will be no easy return to the 1990s and early 2000s, when the UN was at the heart of world events. A new leader will need to reinvent multilateralism in a world where it’s going out of favour.
Depending on the choice they make, we could look back at this decision as the moment that the crumbling international rules-based order began to be rebuilt – or when it slid irretrievably into irrelevance.
- 
  Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize

articles.title: Leftists make waves and Trump flexes muscles: US primary season takeaways
articles.body:
1. Lawmakers fled the House in droves, ensuring a reshaped Congress in 2027Viewed as the chamber of Congress most likely to change hands in the midterms, the House saw significant turnover this cycle, with 74 members departing, the most since 1992, according to a tally from the Pew Research Center. Some outgoing lawmakers retired, while others ran for other offices, but generally didn’t fare particularly well – only 13 made it through primaries for governorships, the Senate or other offices, with the remaining 15 were rejected by voters. Among representatives who sought re-election to the House, 11 lost their primaries, the second-highest total since 2022. Seven of these were Democrats, two of whom – Julie Johnson and Al Green – were unseated by other Democratic incumbents after they were redistricted by Texas Republicans to compete against each other.
 2. Leftists, especially Democratic socialists, rocked the party ...Of the five House Democrats who lost their primaries to newcomers, four were booted by leftist candidates with ties to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). In New York, Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair Adriano Espaillat fell to DSA member Darializa Avila Chevalier and congressman Dan Goldman was ousted by former DSA member Brad Lander, while DSA member Claire Valdez also won the primary to replace retiring congresswoman Nydia Velazquez. In Colorado, DSA member Melat Kiros unseated 30-year incumbent Diana DeGette, and in Michigan, the DSA-endorsed Donovan McKinney beat congressman Shri Thanedar. All are expected to win their seats in the midterms, as their districts are heavily Democratic. “A lot of people were hoping that it was a blip, like oh well, this is a special case,” said the DSA-endorsed Chris Rabb, who is expected to be elected to the House after winning the Democratic primary in deep-blue Philadelphia. “We showed them a different way. So I think all of those things make this election cycle uniquely powerful in ways that most people could not anticipate, myself included.” The fifth sitting Democrat to lose renomination was John Larson. His challenger, Luke Bronin, 47, successfully argued to voters that it was time to replace the 78-year-old incumbent with a younger candidate.
 3. ... but centrists are on the frontlinesThe battle for the House will not be decided in safe blue seats, but rather the 21 districts that the Cook Political Report considers to be toss-ups. In those districts, the nominees are almost entirely backed by the Pacs of either the center-left New Democrat Coalition, or the moderate Blue Dogs, which centrists say bolsters their arguments that their policies most closely align with the voters who determine control of Congress. “If Democrats are to win the majority in the House and/or the Senate, it will be because moderates flip seats from red to blue,” said Matt Bennett, an executive vice-president at the thinktank Third Way. There are exceptions to the trend: former DSA member William Lawrence won the Democratic nomination to take on Republican incumbent Tom Barrett in a swing Michigan congressional district, while in that state’s Democratic Senate primary, Abdul El-Sayed beat congresswoman Haley Stevens, who was backed by much of the party establishment.
 4. Anti-incumbent sentiment among Democrats had its limitsThe DSA’s wins reintensified debate among Democrats over the political direction of the party, but the left-wing movement’s momentum was not absolute. In Missouri, DSA member Cori Bush failed in her primary challenge against congressman Wesley Bell, who had unseated her two years ago. Hawaii congressman Ed Case fended off state senator Jarrett Keohokalole, who had challenged him from the left and argued it was time for generational change. In Massachusetts, congressman Seth Moulton made a similar argument about the Democratic senator Ed Markey, though in this case Moulton was the moderate candidate and Markey the progressive. It didn’t work, and Markey won renomination, as did other congressional Democrats in the state who faced primary challenges. In Colorado, state senator Julie Gonzales mounted an unsuccessful left-wing challenge to Democratic US senator John Hickenlooper, while in Washington, moderate congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez again won the Democratic nomination in her right-leaning district against several challengers.
 5. Trump flexed his muscles, with much successAs always, Trump sought to play kingmaker in the primaries, endorsing candidates who hewed to his agenda and seeking revenge against those who had broken with him, however small their transgressions. Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie lost his primary after the president campaigned against him, and the president’s decision not to make an endorsement in Texas representative Dan Crenshaw’s primary was likely a factor in him losing the Republican nomination. Trump successfully ousted Louisiana senator Bill Cassidy – who voted to convict him after January 6 – as well as Texas senator John Cornyn, for comparatively murkier reasons. The president may rue the latter decision – recent polls have shown the Democratic nominee James Talarico with a slight lead over Trump’s preferred candidate, Ken Paxton. All told, it was a successful primary for Trump – an analysis of his record by USA Today shows nearly 97% of the candidates he backed in congressional and gubernatorial races won their primaries. There were a handful of misses – five gubernatorial candidates won their primaries without Trump’s endorsement, along with four House aspirants.
 6. Aipac spent, for better or worseThe American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) waded into some primaries at a particularly fraught moment for supporters of the Middle Eastern ally. Surveys show that some Republicans and many Democrats now hold negative views of Israel, amid accusations it carried out a genocide in Gaza, and many of the left-wing candidates who ousted Democratic House incumbents did so after attacking their ties to Aipac. Through its United Democracy Project Super Pac, the group nonetheless scored some wins, including Ed Gallrein’s defeat of Massie in Kentucky, Adrian Boafo’s victory in the Maryland primary to replace veteran House Democrat Steny Hoyer, and Bell’s defense against Bush’s primary challenge in Missouri. But the group failed to keep El-Sayed from defeating Rogers in the Michigan Senate primary, despite spending more than $30m in that race, or prevent progressive Aisha Wahab from winning a special election to replace former congressman Eric Swalwell in California.
 7. Some candidates fell to scandals, others pressed onSeveral candidates who ran for office were derailed by scandals. Graham Platner won the Democratic primary to take on veteran Republican senator Susan Collins in Maine, but dropped out amid accusations of sexual assault and misconduct. Swalwell ran for governor of California but exited that race and resigned his US House seat after he, too, was accused of sexual assault. North Carolina Republican congressman Chuck Edwards won his primary but ended his re-election campaign after the House ethics committee said he likely broke rules against sexual harassment, but Republican congressman Max Miller remains in the race amid accusations of domestic violence against his ex-wife. In other instances, the GOP used the primaries to dispose of problematic lawmakers in their ranks. Andy Ogles, a congressman with a history of homophobic and Islamophobic statements, lost in Tennessee after the Republican governor endorsed his challenger and a Super Pac backed by the renewable energy industry spent against him, and scandal-plagued congressman Cory Mills was defeated after other Florida Republicans endorsed his challenger.

articles.title: Russia Claims Cyberattacks Targeted Parliamentary Election Online Voting System
articles.body:
Russian Central Election Commission head Ella Pamfilova claimed that Moscow’s remote electronic voting system suffered a “massive and intense” cyberattack late Saturday night, Sept. 19.
Pamfilova said the attack continued into the morning, according to Reuters and Russian news outlet RBC. However, she maintained that the online voting system operated normally and that the election process was not interrupted.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Moscow City Election Commission head Olga Kirillova also reported increased cyberattacks against the electronic voting system, saying technical teams were working around the clock to counter them.
Russia’s Ministry of Digital Development separately claimed an attempted diversion on communications lines in the Far East. There was no independent verification of the claims, and Russian authorities provided no evidence linking Ukraine to the reported cyber incidents.
Pamfilova added that the overall intensity and complexity of cyberattacks on Russia’s electoral system had grown compared to the 2024 presidential campaign.
Russian parliamentary elections
Russia is holding three-day elections to its 450-seat State Duma from Sept. 18 to 20, marking its first parliamentary vote since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The vote includes polling stations set up in temporarily occupied regions of Ukraine, drawing sharp condemnation from Ukrainian authorities and the international community.
NATO Ready for Any Russian Escalation, Military Chief Says
Independent opposition parties and anti-war candidates have been barred from competing.
On Aug. 10, Russia’s Supreme Court removed the liberal Yabloko party from the ballot following a lawsuit by the Rodina party, eliminating the only competing party running on an explicit anti-war platform. Prominent Yabloko figure Lev Shlosberg remains imprisoned after criticizing the war.
All remaining parties permitted on the ballot – including United Russia, the Communist Party, LDPR, A Just Russia, and New People – support the Kremlin’s policy lines and invasion of Ukraine.
Exiled opposition groups led by Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of opposition leader Alexei Navalny who died in an Arctic prison in 2024, called on Russians to vote against United Russia, while Yabloko urged voters to boycott the process to avoid legitimizing the system.

articles.title: Zelenskyy confirmed an attack on an important oil industry facility in the Moscow region
articles.body:
Zelenskyy confirmed an attack on an important oil industry facility in the Moscow region
Kyiv • UNN
Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that an oil enterprise and a logistics facility of the Russian Federation in the Moscow region had been hit. The attack was carried out using Ukrainian long-range weapons.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that this night, in the Moscow region, Ukrainian warriors struck one of the key enterprises of Russia’s oil industry and the aggressor’s logistics facility. The head of state reported this on Telegram, UNN reports.
Details
"In the Moscow region, our long-range responses had a very tangible impact this night. One of the key enterprises of the Russian oil industry and the aggressor’s logistics facility were struck. These are billions of dollars that support the war machine," the president said.
According to the data provided, the operation involved: FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, "Palianytsia," Vendetta, "Liutyi," "Bars," "Flamingo," "Sichen," Pelican.
"I thank our warriors for their precision: the SBU together with the SBS, SSO, HUR and SZRU. Sanctions were also imposed on an enterprise in the Voronezh region. Moscow should not build layered air-defense rings at the expense of other regions, but should end its brutal war and choose peace. Steps toward de-escalation are on the table—in energy and food security. Political will is needed. I thank everyone who strengthens Ukraine’s long-range capabilities. I am grateful to everyone who complements our long-range responses with sanctions responses. Glory to Ukraine!" Volodymyr Zelenskyy emphasized.
To remind you
Ukrainian FP-1 UAVs struck a Moscow oil refinery, where a fire broke out. The drones also destroyed a warehouse complex in the Moscow region.
